title: A Tiny Spider With a Genome Bigger Than Yours
summary: It is only about the size of a quarter, and it spends its whole life hiding underground. But inside its tiny body, this little spider carries more DNA than a human. The spider is Aptostichus stephencolberti, a trapdoor spider that lives in the coastal dunes of Northern California. Scientists have now sequenced its genome, the complete set of its DNA, and found that it contains 4.6 billion DNA base pairs, roughly 50 percent more than the human genome. It also has 52 chromosomes, compared with 46 in human cells. 'At 4.6 gigabases, or 4.6 billion DNA base pairs, it's not the largest genome among the spiders, but it's significant,' said Jason Bond, a professor at the University of California, Davis, who led the research. The findings were published in the Journal of Heredity, and it is the first time scientists have sequenced the genome of a spider from this family. Trapdoor spiders are secretive hunters. Females spend their entire lives underground in tunnels lined with silk. Each burrow has a hinged door that blends into the sand, so the spider stays hidden while it waits. When an insect wanders close, vibrations give it away, and the spider bursts through its hidden door to grab its meal. Do not worry if you meet one: its venom is not dangerous to people. Of the more than 50,000 known spider species, only about 30 to 50 have venom known to be toxic to humans. The spider's DNA holds another surprise. Spiders lack the usual repetitive DNA found at the ends of chromosomes, in structures called telomeres. That difference may help explain why spider chromosomes seem to evolve faster than those of animals with backbones. The spider's name has a funny backstory. In 2008, television host Stephen Colbert learned that Bond had named a trapdoor spider after rock musician Neil Young. Not wanting to be left out, Colbert demanded a spider of his own on his show, The Colbert Report, in a segment called 'Who's Not Honoring Me Now?' Bond agreed, and Aptostichus stephencolberti was born. The research is part of the California Conservation Genomics project, which collects genetic information to help protect species. That matters for this spider, because rising seas threaten the coastal dunes it calls home.
why_it_matters: Reading the genomes of rare species helps scientists understand how life evolved and how to protect animals whose homes are threatened by rising seas.

background_read: Every living thing carries a genome, the full set of DNA instructions that tells its body how to grow and work, and genomes come in many different sizes.
Spiders are hunters with eight legs, and trapdoor spiders hide in silk-lined burrows with a camouflaged door, waiting to feel the vibrations of prey walking by.
Scientists read genomes to learn how species are related and how they evolved, and the information can also help protect rare animals and the places they live.
